title: tokenizer-runtime-boundary-design-doc-v1
content:
Purpose
This doc captures the current thinking and proposed design for the tokenizer/runtime boundary inside the serving runtime. Scope: tokenization latency visibility, tokenizer caching, batched tokenizers (multi-request tokenization), and how tokenization interacts with the KV cache / scheduling / kernel pipeline. This is an implementation-focused design doc intended for the serving-runtime team and applied-ml stakeholders.

Background & motivation
We currently treat tokenization as a thin client-side step in most deployments (SDKs or customer infra). For hosted and private deployments, however, tokenization happens at multiple locations (client SDK, gateway tier, runtime frontends). We observe three production issues motivating tighter runtime ownership of tokenization:
1) Tokenization latency is a significant portion of cold-start and short-request P95s for short inputs (single-turn completions and instruction prompts).
2) Duplicate tokenization work: identical strings across concurrent requests cause repeated CPU work which becomes a throughput bottleneck at scale.
3) Incorrect cacheability: downstream KV/prefix caches operate on token ids but are often populated with data tokenized by different tokenizer versions/normalization rules, causing cache misses and subtle correctness bugs.

Goals
- Define a stable boundary API between tokenizer and serving runtime that supports multiple tokenizer backends (rust tokenizers, fast-tokenizer C++/Python wrappers, custom user tokenizers).
- Reduce end-to-end P50/P95 for short requests by 20–40ms on average via latency optimizations and batching strategies.
- Avoid duplicated tokenization CPU work through in-memory caching and multi-request batching.
- Provide traceable tokenization metadata (tokenizer version, normalization flags, vocabulary id) so KV/prefix cache keys are stable and debuggable.
- Keep runtime integration minimal for private/on-prem customers that want to supply their own tokenizer binary.

Constraints and non-goals
- We will not reimplement model-specific tokenizers in the runtime for every new architecture. The runtime should be tokenizer-agnostic with a shim interface.
- We will not modify public SDK APIs in this first phase; changes will be opt-in via configuration flags (e.g., server_tokenize=true).
- Security: tokenization must never leak user data outside tenant boundaries; cached tokenization artifacts are per-tenant and encrypted at rest in Dedicated/Private contexts if persisted.

Design components overview
1) Tokenizer interface and metadata
2) Tokenization latency budget and metrics
3) In-memory tokenization cache (per-frontier / per-worker)
4) Batched tokenizer pipeline (coalescing + worker pool)
5) Interaction with KV cache and prefix caching
6) Scheduling and kernel handoff semantics
7) Fallbacks, experiments, and rollout plan

1) Tokenizer interface and metadata
- API shape (flat, language-agnostic):
  - tokenize(input: bytes, options: string_flags) -> { token_ids: [int], token_offsets: [int], tokenizer_meta: string }
  - detokenize(token_ids: [int]) -> bytes (for streaming/debugging tools)
- tokenizer_meta: a compact string tag that must include tokenizer-name/version, normalization flags, vocabulary-hash. Example: "hf-tiktoken@v2|norm=nfkc|vocab_hash=sha1:abc123". This string is used in cache keys and logs.
- Tokenization implementations must be deterministic for identical inputs and options.
- The runtime will ship a reference Rust tokenizer shim (fast, single-threaded) and support loading external tokenizer binaries via a well-known gRPC or unix-socket protocol for Private deployments.

2) Tokenization latency budget and metrics
- Budget: aim for tokenization median <3ms and P95 <15ms for typical short prompts on our reference CPU pool. This is aggressive; initial targets will be 10ms median / 50ms P95 while optimizations roll out.
- Required metrics (per request and aggregated): tokenization_duration_ms, tokenization_source (client/gateway/runtime), tokenizer_meta, token_count, pretokenized_flag (whether client already supplied token ids).
- Tracing: tokenization span should be emitted inside the request trace to attribute CPU/time to tokenization vs scheduling vs GPU kernel.

3) In-memory tokenization cache
Rationale: Many prompts repeat exactly or share prefixes (system prompts, instruction templates). A small LRU cache keyed on (tenant, tokenizer_meta, input_bytes) avoids repeated CPU work.
- Cache key: tenant_id|tokenizer_meta|sha256(input_bytes)
- Cache value: token_ids serialized (compact), token_offsets, stored_as_base64 (or binary memblob).
- Scope/placement: cache is per-runtime-worker process to keep memory bounds predictable and avoid cross-tenant privacy issues. For dedicated pools, process memory limits will be configurable.
- Size: default 128k entries per worker with entry sizing by token_count. Eviction policy: LRU with admission sampling (ignore entries <4 bytes).
- TTL: optional soft TTL 24 hours; configurable per deployment.
- Metrics: cache_hit_ratio, cache_evictions, cache_memory_bytes.
- Correctness: cache items must be invalidated if tokenizer_meta changes. The tokenizer_meta inclusion in key ensures this.

Privacy note: do not persist tokenization cache to disk in multi-tenant hosted environment. Dedicated/Private deployments may optionally persist and encrypt.

4) Batched tokenizer pipeline
Goal: coalesce tokenization requests at the worker frontier to amortize overheads, use vectorized tokenizers when available, and reduce latency tail for concurrent short requests.
- Frontend coalescer: each runtime worker exposes a tokenization queue with a short coalescing window (configurable, default 0–3ms). Requests arriving within the window can be grouped into a batch.
- Grouping semantics: requests with identical tokenizer_meta can be batched together. We will not batch across tokenizer_meta values to avoid incompatibility.
- Batch execution: two modes:
  1) vectorized tokenizer call (preferred): if tokenizer backend supports batch APIs, pass an array of inputs and receive per-input outputs. This requires memory pre-allocation and careful backpressure.
  2) batched CPU worker pool: otherwise, process inputs in parallel across a small pool (N threads) using the same tokenizer instance to exploit shared caches inside the tokenizer library.
- Tail latency: use a hybrid approach: if the coalescing window expires and batch size < threshold, spawn synchronous tokenization to avoid blocking single requests. Threshold default = 8 inputs.
- Backpressure: expose per-worker queue depth; if queue > max (configurable) start rejecting tokenization batching to avoid head-of-line blocking. Rejection falls back to client-side tokenization (if configured) or synchronous per-request tokenization.

5) Interaction with KV cache and prefix caching
- Problem: KV/prefix caches in the runtime operate on token ids. To maintain cache correctness across updates/upgrades, we must:
  - attach tokenizer_meta to any cache keys that depend on token ids (e.g., prefix cache key = tenant|model|tokenizer_meta|prefix_hash).
  - provide normalized prefix extraction APIs: extract_prefix_by_tokens(token_ids, prefix_len) so the cache layer uses token-level primitives rather than byte substrings.
- Population semantics: when a request produces model outputs, the runtime will populate prefix/KV caches using the token_ids returned from tokenize(). This guarantees consistent representation.
- Cache compatibility windows: when we roll tokenizer updates that change tokenization for common strings, we must evict relevant KV caches or create a migration path (e.g., maintain old tokenizer_meta tags for N days and route old-versioned requests to legacy caches). The ops playbook will include a safe migration recipe.

6) Scheduling and kernel handoff semantics
- Tokenization completes before the request is enqueued on the scheduler that assigns model GPU work. This ensures that scheduler decisions (batching, placement) have token_count metadata and can choose appropriate kernel configs (attention kernel selection, kv-cache allocation).
- Pre-tokenized input path: allow clients to send token_ids directly (with tokenizer_meta). The scheduler should trust token_count but must verify tokenizer_meta compatibility against model/vocab expectations.
- Early admission: in some high-throughput flows we may admit requests to a scheduler queue while tokenization is still running (speculative admission). Only allowed if: tokenizer_meta is identical across queued requests and tokenization is guaranteed quickly (<< scheduling_window). This is an optimization to explore but disabled by default.

7) Fallbacks, experiments, and rollout plan
- Phase 0 (opt-in): runtime exposes server_tokenize=false by default. Customers can opt-in per-tenant. Instrument metrics and traces.
- Phase 1 (beta): enable server-side tokenization for hosted non-sensitive tenants. Enable in-memory cache + short coalescing window. Measure latency and CPU.
- Phase 2 (wider rollout): enable for majority of tenants with safeguards (per-tenant CPU budgets), and add per-worker persistent cache in Dedicated deployments.
- Experiments: enable vectorized backend for models where tokenizer library supports batch APIs (measure tokenization throughput improvement). Test coalescing window sizes (0ms/1ms/3ms) and batch size thresholds to find sweet spot.

Implementation notes and TODOs
- Provide a Rust tokenizer shim with the following properties: zero-copy input handling, batch API, deterministic token_offsets. (Owner: Luca Marino)
- Add instrumentation spans around tokenizer calls in the frontend (Owner: Rina Gomez).
- Implement per-worker LRU cache in the runtime core (Owner: Ben Chu). Evaluate existing cache libs vs simple slab allocator.
- Add tokenizer_meta to all cache key builders in prefix/KV cache codepaths (Owner: Maeve O'Neal).
- Add feature flag: server_tokenize per-tenant, and a runtime-config knob for coalescing_window_ms and batch_threshold.
- Benchmark plan: create a synthetic workload with common system prompts and varying concurrency to measure cache hit rate and end-to-end P95. Link: JIRA-RT-4821.

Open questions / risks
- How large should default per-worker cache be to balance memory vs hit-rate? (we should A/B test 32k/128k entries)
- For Private deployments, is it acceptable to allow shared persistent tokenizer cache at the node level? Ops has security concerns.
- Vectorized tokenizer backends may allocate large temporary buffers for batches; how to limit memory amplification under high concurrency?
- Should the runtime attempt to “normalize” inputs (e.g., NFKC) before caching to increase hit rates? This impacts determinism and must be configurable.

Appendix: example cache key canonicalization
- raw input: "Translate to French: Hello" (bytes)
- tokenizer_meta: "hf-tiktoken@v2|norm=nfc|vocab_hash=sha1:9f2"
- key = tenant:acme|hf-tiktoken@v2|sha256(Translate to French: Hello)

Notes to reviewers
- Focus review on the tokenizer_meta shape and the tradeoffs for coalescing window vs tail latency.
- Pay attention to security implications of per-worker caches for multi-tenant hosted deployments.
- If you have a preferred tokenizer library with a batch API, list it in comments (we'll prototype).

References and linked artifacts
- internal confluence: CONFLUENCE-RT/Tokenization-Boundary-Notes
- jira: JIRA-RT-4821 (tokenizer runtime caching experiment)
- github prototype: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/319

Status log
